guide.description: -b:a sets the target audio bitrate — how many kilobits per second the encoded audio uses. Lower bitrates make smaller files at the cost of quality; podcasts and voice are usually fine well below music-quality bitrates. -b:a combines with -ss (skip this many seconds before starting) and -t (stop after this many more seconds) to trim a clip down to a highlight while re-encoding it.

flags.desc: target audio bitrate in kbps, e.g. 128k
skip this many seconds from the start before the output begins
stop the output after this many more seconds

examples.note: skips the first 10s, keeps the next 60s

exercises.title: Set the audio bitrate
exercises.task: Convert podcast-ep1.wav to podcast-ep1-128.mp3 at a bitrate of 128k.
hints: -b:a <rate>k goes between -i <input> and the output file

exercises.title: Trim and set bitrate together
exercises.task: Convert podcast-ep1.wav to highlight.mp3: skip the first 10 seconds, keep the next 60 seconds, at a bitrate of 96k.
hints: -ss skips seconds from the start, -t caps how long the output runs — both can combine with -b:a

exercises.title: Trim from the start with -t alone
exercises.task: Convert podcast-ep1.wav to intro.mp3: keep just the first 120 seconds (no -ss needed since you're starting from the beginning), at a bitrate of 64k.
hints: Without -ss, -t alone just caps the output length from the very start

exercises.title: Put it together: convert, then verify with ffprobe
exercises.task: Convert podcast-ep1.wav to highlight2.mp3 the same way as before (skip 10s, keep 60s, 96k bitrate), then use ffprobe to print its summary and confirm the settings took effect.
hints: Convert first, then run ffprobe on the file you just created
ffmpeg -i podcast-ep1.wav -ss 10 -t 60 -b:a 96k highlight2.mp3, then ffprobe highlight2.mp3
